characteristics prepared via a choice of chemical deposition or vacuum 
thermal evaporation
Priyanka Bamola , Fabiola De Bray S´anchez , M.T.S. Nair , P.K. Nair *
Instituto de Energías Renovables, Universidad Nacional Aut´onoma de M´exico Temixco, Morelos, 62580, Mexico

Solar cells
Chemical deposition
Thermal evaporation
A B S T R A C T
Antimony sulfide selenide solar cells, FTO/CdS/Sb2Sx1Se3-x1/Sb2Sx2Se3-x2/graphite-Ag, of above 5 % conversion 
efficiency (η), open circuit voltage (VOC) 0.45 V and short circuit current density (JSC) 24 mA cm – 2, were ob­
tained for Sb2SxSe3-x (160–350 nm) of variable bandgap (Eg) 1.25–1.5 eV prepared by chemical deposition (CD) 
or thermal evaporation (TE). Commercial SnO2:F (FTO) was coated first with a CdS thin film. For CD - Sb2SxSe3-x 
absorbers, selenosulfate and thioacetamide were at a molar ratio 0.1:3 for the first deposition, and 1:3 in the 
second deposition (film thickness, 160 nm). In TE, Sb2Se3-Sb2S3 was in 1:3 ratio in the first crucible, and distinct 
in the second (film thickness, 300 nm). CD-Solar cells had η, 5.2 %, JSC 23.6 mA cm – 2 and VOC of 0.41 V and the 
TE-solar cells, 5.75 %, 24.5 mA cm – 2 and 0.45 V, respectively. Thus, Sb2SxSe3-x of variable Eg provides a higher 
VOC and conserves JSC.
1. Introduction
During the years 2009–2022, antimony sulfide selenide Sb2(SxSe1-x)3 
solar cells have established themselves as a research and development (R 
& D) theme, with the solar to electric energy conversion efficiency (η) of 
these solar cells steadily improving from less than 1 % in 2009 to above 
10.5 % by the year 2020 [1]. The versatility of these materials for solar 
cell technologies merits attention: (i) the optical bandgap (Eg) of these 
materials may be continuously varied from 1.1 eV (Sb2Se3) to 1.88 eV 
(Sb2S3) [2], falling within the interval of successful thin film solar cell 
technologies [3,4]; (ii) the materials may be prepared using different 
thin film methods offering comparable values for η [1]; (iii) the opera­
tional stability of the solar cells are exceptionally good [5]; (iv) if a 
device structure obtained through R & D on these solar cells takes η 
toward 20 %, material availability makes large scale commercial pro­
duction of the modules feasible [1]. Improvement of η of these cells 
toward such a level requires specific attention to improve the 
Sb2(SxSe1-x)3 materials through “extrinsic doping” at the lattice sites, 
defect passivation within the material and at the interfaces in the solar 
cell structure [6–9]. The successful approach of “bandgap engineering” 
to create a “V-profile of Eg” across the absorber film as in Cu-In-Ga-S-Se 
cells [3], is readily applicable in Sb2(SxSe1-x)3 solar cells [10].

proportional variation with x is shown in Fig. 1. The variation in the

graphite-silver is also shown. The data pertain to solar cells prepared by 
thermal evaporation of powder mixes of Sb2S3-Sb2Se3, adapted from 
Ref. [5]. The data points for Eg, except for Sb2Se3 (x = 0) and Sb2S3 (x =
1) taken from Ref. [2], are from experimental results reported there. In 
these solar cells with no extrinsic doping in the absorber or window film 
(CdS), at low values of x close to 0.2, a high JSC of above 30 mA cm – 2 is 
obtained with η of 6.8 %, but its VOC is low, 0.42 V. With x of 0.7, a VOC of 
0.56 V is available in the solar cell, but its low JSC of 12 mA cm – 2 results 
in a low η of 2.5 %. The benefit of graded band gap absorber in these 
solar cells is apparent for these results. Solar cells of SnO2:F (FTO)/CdS

2. Experimental
2.1. Development of the solar cell device structure
In both CD and VTE methods, the basic device structure remained the 
same, as described in Fig. 2i. Clear sheet glass of 2.2 mm in thickness 
with a transparent electrically conductive coating (TEC 7, fluorine- 
doped SnO2 or FTO) with a sheet resistance of 7 Ω was supplied in 30 
cm × 30 cm size sheets from Greatcell Solar Materials (Australia). These 
were cut to 7.5 cm × 2.5 cm in size, cleaned with cotton swabs dipped in 
a neutral soap solution, rinsed and dried.
2.1.1. Chemical reagents and thin film deposition
Laboratory reagents of 98–99 % assay supplied by Sigma – Aldrich or 
Fermont (Mexico) were used for preparing the solar cells described in 
Fig. 2. The colloidal graphite paint and the silver paint were purchased 
from SPI (USA). Solutions of different substances were prepared in de- 
ionized water at the concentrations (mol dm – 3 = M) mentioned for 
the chemical deposition of the different thin films. Sodium selenosulfate, 
Na2SeSO3, of 0.4 M in concentration with concurrent presence of 0.4 M 
of Na2SO3 was prepared by refluxing Na2SO3 and elemental Se in 100 
mL water, described below.
2.1.2. CdS thin film deposition
A CdS thin film of 80–100 nm in thickness, appearing in reflected 
light as a golden-purple layer on the glass-side of the FTO was made by 
chemical deposition at 80 ◦C during 55–70 min, as described in Fig. 2ii. 
A methodology reported previously [12] was used: To a 100 mL glass 
beaker, the following aqueous solutions were sequentially added with 
stirring: cadmium nitrate (20 mL, 0.1 M or mol dm – 3), sodium citrate 
(12 mL, 1 M), ammonia aq. (1.6 mL, 16 M), thiourea (4 mL, 1 M), and 
42.4 mL of deionized water. At a temperature of 80 ◦C, a film of 80 nm

graphite-silver solar cells prepared by vacuum thermal evaporation of Sb2S3-Sb2Se3 powder mix, with a fixed value of x and of Eg along the absorber thickness,

transparent solution, which would remain stable upon storage for two 
months without segregation of elemental Se from Na2SeSO3. The for­
mation of elemental Se0 from (Se2−) in contact with atmospheric oxygen 
(O2 + Se2 – → O2
2 – + Se0) is inhibited in the presence of SO3
2 –, which
